slides.title: From RTL to GDSII: how a digital chip gets made
slides.lead: A ten-stage tour for students who know logic gates and flip-flops but have never seen a chip design flow.

slides.title: What you will be able to explain afterwards

bullets.text: Name the stages a design passes through, in order.
Say, for each stage, what goes in, what comes out, and what is checked.
Explain setup and hold violations, and the four signoff checks.

slides.title: What is an ASIC, and what is a design flow?

bullets.text: An ASIC is silicon manufactured to carry out one specific function.
The design flow: the steps from an idea to the data used for fabrication.
Each step is supported by electronic design automation (EDA) tools.
The work can last months; a proven flow keeps it on schedule.
From synthesis to the final layout file, it can run automatically.

slides.title: The flow at a glance: five steps

bullets.text: Design entry: describe the design in a hardware description language.
Functional verification: confirm it behaves as required.
Synthesis: convert the description into a netlist.
Physical implementation: turn the netlist into a layout by floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, and routing.
Signoff: final checks before manufacturing.
HDL (hardware description language): describes hardware; Verilog is one. RTL (register-transfer level): a high-level way of describing a circuit.
Netlist: standard cells and macros, and their connections.
Cell: another name for a CMOS logic gate.
A standard cell library typically has several sizes of one cell.
PDK (process design kit): files that describe one fabrication process to the tools.

slides.title: Stage 1: Specification
slides.lead: One project's process (OpenTitan): the first of three broad stages.

bullets.text: A concept is written up as a brief proposal and goes through a request for comment.
After review, the full detailed specification is completed.
It is published to the wider team and refined from their comments.
Checked by: up to three reviews, one a potential security review.
The design is written in an HDL such as Verilog, normally at RTL.
Only a subset of Verilog can be synthesized.
Clocked logic uses non-blocking assignments; purely combinational logic uses blocking ones.
Flip-flops are used in place of latches unless a latch is absolutely necessary.
Risk: simulation and synthesis disagreeing.
Goal: the design under test (DUT) behaves as its requirements say.
Simulation and formal verification are combined.
Both the RTL and, later, the gate-level netlist are verified.
Testing starts with a basic smoke test; stress tests exercise several features at once. All simulations run regularly as a regression.
In OpenTitan, done: every checklist item of every verification stage is ticked.

slides.title: When have we tested enough? Coverage

bullets.text: Coverage answers the question of when testing is done.
Code coverage: extracted automatically by the simulator from lines, branches, and other structures.
Functional coverage: cover points that an engineer has to write.
Full code coverage shows all code ran, not that it does the right thing; both kinds are needed.
Gaps are closed with more tests or waived: coverage closure.
In: the Verilog files and the timing constraints (an SDC file).
Software turns a higher-level description into a lower-level one that behaves the same.
Out: a netlist, a circuit built from logic cells.
Two challenges: optimize the netlist, and map it onto gate types that physically exist.
Optimization can target area or timing; results are verified again by simulation.
In: a size target for the design.
I/O pins are placed on the boundary.
Macros are placed, and tap cells are added: non-functional cells that tie the well or substrate.
A power grid is created.
Checked by: IR drop analysis. IR drop is the voltage lost in the power grid on the way to the cells.
In: a placement density, from 0 (widely spread) to 1 (tightly packed).
The flow's steps include global placement, detailed placement, and timing optimization with a resizer.
A repair step inserts buffers to fix maximum slew, capacitance, and fanout violations, and resizes gates.
Placement options affect area and timing.
Side effect: timing optimization enlarges the design.

slides.title: Timing in one slide: setup, hold, slack

bullets.text: A flip-flop needs stable input before the clock edge (setup time) and after (hold time).
Setup violation: data arrives after it is required. Hold: before.
Slack: the margin between required and actual arrival time; it must be positive.
A violation shows up as negative slack; the flip-flop can go metastable.
Static timing analysis (STA) computes these times on every path.
In: the placed design. Out: a well-balanced clock tree.
Clock buffers are inserted to balance the tree.
Clock skew: the clock arrives at different flip-flops at different times.
Skew is the main cause of hold violations, so it is reported and fixed.
Timing repair for setup and hold runs after this stage.
Two passes: a design must pass global routing without violations before detailed routing.
Global routing allocates the routing resources.
Detailed routing includes search and repair and its own DRC (design rule checking) engine.
Checked by: zero violations, and an antenna check: a long wire can collect charge during fabrication and damage a transistor gate.
Problem: congestion stops global routing.
The automated flow calls its last stage layout generation.
Metal fill adds floating metal shapes so that density rules are met.
Parasitics extraction computes the resistance and capacitance of the routed wires.
Out: the final layout in GDSII form.
Final timing is reported as worst slack, total negative slack, and worst negative slack.

slides.title: Stage 10: Signoff
slides.lead: Physical and timing verification before manufacturing.

bullets.text: DRC (design rule checking): the layout against the foundry's manufacturing rules.
LVS (layout versus schematic): both have the same connectivity.
STA: on the fully implemented design.
Antenna check: looks for antenna violations.
Then tape-out: the design goes to a fabrication facility.

slides.title: Where the sources disagree
slides.lead: S1, S2, … are the sources under each slide.

bullets.text: Physical implementation: one step (S2), or separate stages (S1).
The end: signoff (S2), or no stage of that name (S1).
Signoff: layout checks (S2), a verification review (S10), a project stage (S8).
DRC: a signoff step (S2), or a post-routing report (S1).
Timing closure: a process (S3), or a state (S4).

slides.title: The whole flow on one page, and what our sources do not cover
slides.lead: The flow in four sentences, and what is missing.

bullets.text: Describe the design in a hardware description language and verify it.
Synthesis converts the description into a netlist.
Physical implementation turns the netlist into a layout.
Signoff checks the layout; then tape-out.
Gaps in our sources: no definition of coverage or of a standard cell library; nothing on routing inputs.
What does synthesis take in, and what does it produce? (slide 10)
Which arrives too late: data in a setup or a hold violation? (slide 13)
What is clock skew, and which violation is it the main cause of? (slide 14)
Which signoff check compares layout with schematic? (slide 17)
